summary: This Informational document defines Post-Quantum Traditional hybrid key exchange methods for SSH transport that combine ML-KEM with elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman.

eli5.summary: SSH gets a double lock: one new and quantum-resistant, one tried and tested.

subtitle: Combining quantum-resistant and traditional key exchange in SSH

tldr.problem: Current SSH key exchange relies on elliptic curve mathematics that quantum computers could break, enabling harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks where adversaries record encrypted sessions today to decrypt them later.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines hybrid key exchange methods for SSH that combine ML-KEM (a quantum-resistant key encapsulation mechanism) with traditional elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, so the session is secure if either method is unbroken.
tldr.outcome: Three hybrid methods are defined for SSH: mlkem768nistp256-sha256, mlkem1024nistp384-sha384, and mlkem768x25519-sha256, enabling post-quantum cryptography in SSH deployments.

facts.label: Classical key exchanges
facts.value: ECDH with P-256, P-384, or X25519

today: RFC 10042 is an Informational document enabling post-quantum cryptography in SSH deployments. It has been implemented in OpenSSH and is used by organizations preparing SSH for the quantum era. RFC 4253 (SSH transport) and RFC 9794 (PQ/T terminology) provide context and standards for the hybrid approach.

sections.title: The Quantum Threat to SSH and Hybrid Solution
sections.content:
SSH (Secure Shell) currently uses elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) for key exchange, a scheme whose security rests on the computational difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem. However, sufficiently large quantum computers could solve this problem in polynomial time, rendering recorded encrypted SSH sessions vulnerable to decryption. An attacker following a "harvest now, decrypt later" strategy could record encrypted SSH traffic today and decrypt it when quantum computers become available.

This document addresses this threat by extending SSH's key exchange with Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) hybrid methods that combine a quantum-resistant Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) called ML-KEM with traditional ECDH. If either key exchange method remains secure, the session is secure. This provides a migration path to post-quantum cryptography without requiring all systems to break away from well-tested classical methods.
sections.eli5: Someone could record your SSH conversation today and wait 20 years to decode it with a quantum computer. A hybrid lock protects you: an attacker would need to break both the new quantum-resistant method and the old one.

sections.title: ML-KEM and the Hybrid Abstraction
sections.content:
The post-quantum mechanism in this specification is ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), standardized by NIST in 2024. A KEM is a cryptographic primitive with three operations: KeyGen (generates a public key and secret key), Encaps (takes a public key and produces a ciphertext and shared secret), and Decaps (takes a secret key and ciphertext and recovers the shared secret).

In a hybrid SSH key exchange, the client generates both an ML-KEM public key (C_PK2) and an ECDH public key (C_PK1), and sends both to the server. The server generates an ECDH public key (S_PK1) and uses the client's ML-KEM public key to generate a ciphertext (S_CT2) via Encaps. The server sends both S_PK1 and S_CT2 back. Both sides then have two shared secrets: K_CL from ECDH and K_PQ from ML-KEM decapsulation. These are combined via hashing to produce the final session key K.
sections.eli5: Both client and server do two key-exchange dances: one with the new quantum-resistant method and one with the old way. The final key is made from both.

sections.title: Three Hybrid Method Definitions
sections.content:
The document defines three concrete hybrid key exchange method names for SSH negotiation. mlkem768nistp256-sha256 pairs ML-KEM-768 with NIST P-256 and uses SHA-256 for hashing. mlkem1024nistp384-sha384 pairs ML-KEM-1024 with NIST P-384 and uses SHA-384. mlkem768x25519-sha256 pairs ML-KEM-768 with Curve25519 and uses SHA-256.

The choices reflect different security levels and practical considerations. ML-KEM-768 provides level 3 post-quantum security (roughly equivalent to 128-bit symmetric key strength), while ML-KEM-1024 provides level 5 (roughly equivalent to 256-bit). X25519 is preferred by many implementations for side-channel resistance and performance, while NIST curves are sometimes preferred for regulatory compliance. The HASH function used in key derivation is specified by the method name.
sections.eli5: SSH now supports three new lock combinations you can choose from, with different strength levels.

sections.title: Combining Shared Secrets and Key Derivation
sections.content:
After exchanging keys, the two shared secrets K_CL (from ECDH) and K_PQ (from ML-KEM) must be combined into a single session key K. This specification uses the simple combiner K = HASH(K_PQ || K_CL), where the post-quantum secret is hashed together with the classical secret and the result is used in SSH's standard key derivation process.

A critical implementation detail: both K_CL and K_PQ are encoded as fixed-length byte arrays (not as multi-precision integers as in traditional SSH), and K itself is encoded as a string. This fixed-length encoding prevents side-channel attacks that could leak information about the most significant bits of the secret. The exchange hash H, used to derive encryption and authentication keys, incorporates C_INIT (the client's public keys), S_REPLY (the server's public key and ciphertext), and K, following the standard SSH key exchange flow.
sections.eli5: The two secrets are mixed together with a hash function in a way that does not leak information through timing side channels.

sections.title: Security Assumptions and Validation
sections.content:
The security of the hybrid methods depends on both ML-KEM and the chosen classical key exchange (ECDH or X25519) remaining secure. The specification requires that ephemeral key pairs be generated fresh for each connection and that randomness not be reused across ML-KEM encapsulations, as the security of the protocol depends on cryptographically strong random data.

Notably, both client and server must validate the length and content of received public keys and ciphertexts to prevent length extension attacks. The client must check that S_REPLY has the expected length before decapsulating, and the server must check that C_INIT has the expected length before encapsulating. If checks fail, either party must abort with a disconnect message. The security proofs in related research show that the protocol achieves both IND-CPA (passive attacker) and IND-CCA2 (active attacker) security, contingent on the underlying primitives and assumptions about the hash function.
sections.eli5: Each time you connect, use fresh keys and good randomness. Check that messages have the right size before decoding them.
